{{short description|Galaxies bound to the Milky Way}}
The [[Milky Way]] has several smaller [[Satellite galaxy|galaxies gravitationally bound to it]], as part of the Milky Way [[Galaxy group|subgroup]], which is part of the local galaxy cluster, the [[Local Group]].<ref>{{cite journal |title= An Eclectic View of our Milky Way Galaxy |author= David G. Turner |date= 15 August 2013 |publication-date= September 2013 |journal= Canadian Journal of Physics |volume= 92 |issue= 9 |pages= 959–963 |doi= 10.1139/cjp-2013-0429 |bibcode= 2014CaJPh..92..959T |arxiv= 1310.0014 |s2cid= 118390693 }}</ref>

There are 61 small galaxies confirmed to be within {{convert|420|kpc|e6ly|abbr=off|lk=on}} of the Milky Way,<ref name="satellitecensus" /> but not all of them are necessarily in orbit, and some may themselves be in orbit of other satellite galaxies. The only ones visible to the naked eye are the [[Large Magellanic Cloud|Large]] and [[Small Magellanic Cloud|Small]] Magellanic Clouds, which have been observed since prehistory. Measurements with the Hubble Space Telescope in 2006 suggest the Magellanic Clouds may be moving too fast to be orbiting the Milky Way.<ref>{{cite web|title=Press release: Magellanic Clouds May Be Just Passing Through|url=https://www.cfa.harvard.edu/news/2007-02|publisher=Harvard University|date=January 9, 2007}}</ref> Of the galaxies confirmed to be in orbit, the largest is the [[Sagittarius Dwarf Spheroidal Galaxy]], which has a diameter of {{convert|2.6|kpc|ly}}<ref name="Karachentsev et al. 2004">{{cite journal
  |last1      = Karachentsev |first1 = I. D.
  |last2      = Karachentseva |first2 = V. E.
  |last3      = Hutchmeier |first3= W. K.
  |last4      = Makarov |first4= D. I.
  |title      = A Catalog of Neighboring Galaxies
  |journal    = [[The Astronomical Journal]]
  |date       = 2004
  |volume     = 127
  |issue      = 4
  |pages      = 2031–2068
  |bibcode    = 2004AJ....127.2031K
  |doi        = 10.1086/382905 |doi-access= free
  }}</ref> or roughly a twentieth that of the Milky Way.

==Characteristics==
Satellite galaxies that orbit from {{convert|1000|ly|pc|abbr=on|lk=on}} of the edge of the [[disc (galaxy)|disc]] of the Milky Way Galaxy to the edge of the [[dark matter halo]] of the Milky Way at {{tooltip|{{convert|300|kpc|ly|abbr=on|order=flip}}|virial radius of our galaxy}} from the center of the galaxy,{{efn|The distance to edge of the dark matter halo of the galaxy from its center is the virial radius of a galaxy, R<sub>vir</sub>}} are generally depleted in hydrogen gas compared to those that orbit more distantly. This is because of their interactions with the dense hot gas halo of the Milky Way that strip cold gas from the satellites. Satellites beyond that region still retain copious quantities of gas.<ref>{{cite news |url= http://www.spacedaily.com/reports/Milky_Way_Ransacks_Nearby_Dwarf_Galaxies_Stripping_All_Traces_of_Star_Forming_Gas_999.html |publisher= SpaceDaily |date= 17 October 2014 |title= Milky Way Ransacks Nearby Dwarf Galaxies}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2014/10/141015152552.htm |publisher= ScienceDaily |date= 15 October 2014 |title= Milky Way ransacks nearby dwarf galaxies}}</ref>

==Streams==
{{See also|List of stellar streams}}
The Sagittarius Dwarf Spheroidal Galaxy is currently in the process of being [[Interacting galaxy|consumed]] by the Milky Way and is expected to pass through it within the next 100 million years. The [[Sagittarius Stream]] is a stream of stars in polar orbit around the Milky Way leeched from the Sagittarius Dwarf. The [[Virgo Stellar Stream]] is a stream of stars that is believed to have once been an orbiting dwarf galaxy that has been completely distended by the Milky Way's gravity.
